title: Diplopia - Binocular Diplopia from Diabetic Cranial Neuropathy
patient_instructions: You are Mary, a 58-year-old woman who has come in because you have been seeing double for the past week. Open with: 'Doctor, I keep seeing two of things, it's really strange and it's the first time.' Key scripted finding for the cover test: when the candidate covers or asks you to close EITHER eye, the double vision gets BETTER and goes away; with both eyes open you see double. The double images are side by side (horizontal) and it is worse when you look towards your right. No pain in or around the eye, no headache, no vomiting, no limb weakness or numbness, no speech or walking problems. It is NOT worse at the end of the day and not helped by rest. No eyelid drooping. You have type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, but you often forget to take it and you have not seen your GP or had your eyes checked for a long time. You also have high blood pressure on perindopril. No thyroid problems, no trauma, no recent illness. Your idea: 'maybe I need new glasses.' Your concern: 'is it a stroke or a brain tumour?' Your expectation: to find out what is wrong. Affect: worried, cooperative. Cooperate fully with any eye-movement examination the candidate performs.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a general practice. Mary, 58, presents with double vision for one week. Over 8 minutes, perform a focused ocular-motility and relevant cranial-nerve examination (you may narrate what you are testing and ask the patient the cover question), interpret your findings, and explain to the patient your most likely diagnosis and differential diagnoses. An examination findings card is available from the examiner on request.
examiner_instructions: This station tests whether the candidate can separate monocular from binocular diplopia with the cover test and localise a binocular (ocular-motility) problem. The scripted/card finding is: diplopia resolves when EITHER eye is covered (binocular), horizontal image separation worse on right gaze, i.e. a right sixth-nerve (lateral rectus) palsy, on a background of poorly controlled diabetes with 3+ glucosuria - a microvascular diabetic cranial neuropathy. Ensure correct nerve-muscle mapping: CN VI supplies the LATERAL rectus (abduction) causing horizontal diplopia; CN III supplies medial/superior/inferior rectus and inferior oblique; CN IV supplies superior oblique (vertical/torsional diplopia). The critical safety point: a PUPIL-INVOLVING, painful third-nerve palsy suggests a compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm - a neurosurgical emergency needing urgent CT/CT-angiography - whereas microvascular CN III palsy is typically pupil-sparing. Provide the card (VA, pupils, H-pattern motility, lids) on request. Prompt once if the pupil is not assessed: 'What did you find with the pupils?'

criteria: Introduces self, consents, and clarifies diplopia versus blurred vision
Performs/asks the cover test correctly (double vision resolves when either eye covered = binocular)
Characterises image separation (horizontal vs vertical), worsening gaze, distance vs near, end-of-day worsening and head position
Structured ocular-motility exam (H-pattern), assesses visual acuity, pupils (including RAPD), lids (ptosis/fatigability), and thyroid eye signs
Correctly identifies binocular diplopia and localises a sixth-nerve (lateral rectus) palsy with horizontal separation
Attributes to microvascular diabetic cranial neuropathy using cover test, poor diabetic control and 3+ glucosuria
Gives a localised differential along the pathway (brain: tumour/MS/stroke; NMJ: myasthenia; muscle: thyroid eye disease/blow-out; monocular causes)
Assesses the pupil and recognises pupil-involving painful CN III palsy suggests a compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm needing urgent CT/CT-angiography
States sudden diplopia with headache, altered consciousness or pupil-involving CN III warrants urgent neuroimaging
Management of microvascular cause: HbA1c, optimise glycaemic and BP control, medication adherence, GP/eye-clinic follow-up (most microvascular palsies recover in weeks-months)
Explains binocular diplopia and the diabetes link in plain language and checks understanding
Addresses patient's fear of stroke/tumour honestly and safety-nets

red_flags: Pupil-involving (fixed dilated), painful third-nerve palsy - suspect compressive posterior communicating artery aneurysm; neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent CT/CT-angiography
Sudden binocular diplopia with headache, vomiting or altered consciousness - urgent neuroimaging to exclude aneurysm, stroke or space-occupying lesion
Diplopia with focal neurology (limb weakness/numbness, dysarthria, ataxia) or internuclear ophthalmoplegia - central/brainstem cause (stroke, MS)
Painful diplopia with proptosis and lid signs - orbital/thyroid pathology or orbital apex lesion
Fatigable ptosis and end-of-day diplopia - myasthenia gravis (risk of bulbar/respiratory involvement)
australian_guidelines: Murtagh diplopia diagnostic strategy - office cover test: if diplopia persists with each eye occluded it is uniocular; if it disappears when either eye is covered there is an ocular-movement (binocular) defect; consider the seven masquerades (diabetes mononeuritis, thyroid)
Talley & O'Connor Clinical Examination - cranial-nerve/eye-movement examination, including internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failed adduction with abducting-eye nystagmus) as a brainstem/MS sign
RACGP / Therapeutic Guidelines - management of type 2 diabetes: assess HbA1c, optimise glycaemic control and adherence, screen for microvascular complications and arrange regular eye review
eTG / neurology - urgent neuroimaging (CT/CT-angiography) for a pupil-involving third-nerve palsy to exclude aneurysm
learning_objectives: Use the cover test to distinguish monocular from binocular diplopia
Correctly map cranial nerves III, IV and VI to their extraocular muscles and diplopia patterns
Recognise the pupil-sparing vs pupil-involving distinction in third-nerve palsy as a must-not-miss safety point
Formulate a localised differential and management plan for diabetic microvascular cranial neuropathy
key_points: Binocular diplopia resolves when either eye is covered; monocular diplopia (e.g. cataract, astigmatism) persists with the fellow eye covered.
CN VI palsy = lateral rectus weakness = horizontal diplopia worse on gaze to the affected side; CN III/IV cause vertical/torsional diplopia.
A pupil-involving, painful third-nerve palsy is a compressive aneurysm until proven otherwise - urgent CT-angiography; microvascular CN III palsy is usually pupil-sparing.
Diabetic microvascular cranial neuropathies are usually painless, pupil-sparing and recover over weeks to months with glycaemic optimisation.

citations.claim: The office cover test distinguishes uniocular from binocular diplopia - if double vision persists with each eye occluded it is uniocular; if it disappears when either eye is covered there is a defect of one of the muscles moving the eyeball; consider the seven masquerades (diabetes mononeuritis, thyroid).
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.215

citations.claim: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (failed adduction on lateral gaze with nystagmus of the abducting eye) is a brainstem sign, and vertical corrections suggest other ocular, neuromuscular or central pathology - relevant to examining eye movements and the MS differential.
citations.source: Talley and O'Connor's Clinical Examination, 8th edition, p.515

citations.claim: Cranial-nerve examination underpins the localisation of diplopia and ptosis (AMC cranial-nerve examination reference supporting the structured approach).
citations.source: AMC Handbook of Clinical Assessment.pdf, p.518
